text:
Good morning everyone. I found Q3 quite granular – deciding on acceptability thresholds for each data point felt a bit artificial. It’s hard to assess improvement without knowing *how* significantly performance increases with each addition.

For me, explainability (Q4) is paramount. As advisors, we need to understand the basis of any flags to have meaningful conversations with students. Low or very low explainability isn't acceptable. 

I was a little surprised by the strong 'never' responses regarding age, gender and race/ethnicity – I think there’s a fear of reinforcing bias, which is valid. Perhaps an opt-out mechanism could address this alongside rigorous fairness testing? My 'moderate' response for first-gen status reflected believing it *could* be relevant with careful interpretation but not without considering potential biases.

Good morning. I agree with A1 about Q3 feeling a bit artificial – it’s hard to quantify ‘improvement’ without knowing the actual impact on accuracy. It felt like guessing.

For me, the biggest thing is explainability too, especially given my dyslexia. Being flagged for something I don't understand would be really frustrating and unhelpful. That’s why I went with 'small' improvement only for high explainability. 

I was surprised to see so many ‘nevers’ on sensitive data, but I get it. My responses were stricter because of my own experiences – I worry about being *defined* by those factors. But the idea of an opt-out is excellent; that could alleviate some concerns and allow students to control their data.

Good morning everyone. I agree with A1 and S7 about the granularity of Q3; it’s challenging to assess incremental improvements without more context on predictive power. As an advisor, I see those questions as hypotheticals – real-world impact is what matters.

I think Q5, regarding fairness, is arguably *the* most important. We absolutely must prioritize equal recall across groups, even if it means a small dip in overall accuracy. Identifying all students who need support, regardless of background, has to be the goal. 

My responses on sensitive data reflect that. I marked 'never' because without incredibly robust safeguards against bias – and simply assuming those exist isn’t enough – including them feels ethically problematic. An opt-out is a good start, but proactive transparency is essential too.

Good morning everyone. I agree with what’s been said about Q3 feeling quite abstract – imagining improvements without knowing *how* much each data point actually helps feels difficult. It's hard to weigh those small increases against privacy concerns.

I think Q5, fairness, is also incredibly important. Seeing ‘equal recall’ being so strongly supported is reassuring. As someone who restarted a programme, I really appreciate the emphasis on not overlooking anyone due to their background. 

My stricter responses on sensitive data – mostly “never” – come from personal experience and feeling vulnerable as an international student. While opt-outs are good, robust safeguards and transparent use of any data are vital before I'd feel comfortable with it being included at all.

Good morning everyone. I largely agree with what’s been said – Q3 *did* feel hypothetical, and estimating improvement without knowing the actual impact is tricky. As an advisor for eleven years, I'm used to making judgements based on a holistic view of the student; breaking it down into these data points felt artificial.

I think Q5 regarding fairness is absolutely critical. We *must* prioritize equal recall. From my experience, students from certain backgrounds are already less likely to seek help – we can’t exacerbate that with a biased system. 

My responses on sensitive data reflected the need for caution; I see value in understanding first-generation status or financial aid *context*, but only if it genuinely helps identify support needs and doesn't lead to profiling. The opt-out idea is good, though transparency about *why* data is being requested is paramount.

Good morning everyone. I agree with a lot of what’s been said – Q3 did feel quite detached from reality, trying to assess improvement without knowing the actual impact on the model's performance. As a student juggling work and studies, I found it hard to imagine those small percentage improvements making a real difference. 

For me, explainability is also key. Being flagged for something opaque would be stressful – especially as an international student navigating a new system. While fairness (Q5) is obviously crucial, I think the biggest tension lies in balancing privacy with accuracy. My stricter responses on sensitive data reflect that; I’m wary of being categorized. The opt-out mechanism sounds good, but transparency about *how* the university uses this information is vital for building trust.

Good morning everyone. I agree with a lot of what’s been said – Q3 felt very hypothetical. Trying to judge improvements without knowing *how* much each data point actually helps was difficult, especially thinking about the real-world impact on students.

For me, explainability is really important, perhaps even more so because I restarted my studies after dropping out once before. Being flagged for something I don’t understand feels… judgemental, and unhelpful. That's why I wanted a clear improvement for higher explainability. My stricter answers on sensitive data reflect that – as an international student, I worry about being labelled or misunderstood. An opt-out is good, but transparency about *why* this data is even collected is crucial for building trust.

Good morning everyone. I agree with a lot of what’s been said – especially about Q3 feeling abstract and hypothetical. It's hard to gauge improvement without knowing how much each data point actually *helps*.

For me, though, the biggest thing is probably explainability (Q4). As someone diagnosed with ADHD who previously dropped out, I worry a lot about being misjudged or misunderstood. Being flagged for something opaque would feel incredibly invalidating. 

I was stricter on sensitive data because of this – my history means I’m already hyper-aware of how labels can affect perceptions. An opt-out is vital, but even then, complete transparency is key; I need to understand *why* any data point is being used about me.

Good morning everyone. I agree with a lot of what's been said – Q3 did feel quite removed from real life, trying to assess improvement without knowing how much each data point actually *adds*. As someone finishing my Masters but having struggled with pace due to my long-term health condition, the hypothetical nature felt… distant.

For me, explainability is hugely important. Being flagged based on something I don't understand would be incredibly stressful and invalidate my efforts. My stricter responses regarding sensitive data reflect my vulnerability – as an international student *and* someone managing a chronic illness, I’m wary of being categorized or misunderstood. An opt-out is essential, but transparency about data use is paramount for building trust; knowing *why* something flags me is vital.

Good morning everyone. I agree with many points already raised – Q3 definitely felt abstract, trying to imagine improvements without knowing how much each data point would actually help. As a first-year Masters student still adjusting to the Danish system, it was hard to assess that realistically.

For me, explainability is also crucial. Coming from another country, navigating a new academic culture is already challenging enough. Being flagged for something I don't understand would feel isolating and unhelpful. My stricter responses on sensitive data – particularly nationality – reflect that vulnerability. While an opt-out sounds good, clear transparency about *how* the university uses this information is vital to build trust and make me feel comfortable.

Good morning everyone. I agree with a lot of what’s been said – Q3 felt very hypothetical; it was hard to picture real improvements without knowing *how* much each data point would actually contribute. As someone managing a chronic health condition while finishing my Masters, that distance from reality really struck me.

I think explainability is absolutely essential. Being flagged for something I don’t understand, especially given my health challenges already feel isolating. My stricter responses on sensitive data reflect feeling vulnerable; disability-related information needs particularly careful handling. An opt-out is good, but genuine transparency about *why* this data's collected and used is vital to build trust - as a student, I want to understand how it affects me.

Good morning everyone. I agree with a lot of what’s been said – Q3 *did* feel quite removed from real life, and assessing improvements without knowing how much each data point actually helps was hard. It's easy to say 'moderate improvement', but harder to visualise that in practice.

For me, explainability is really important, partly because I dropped out once before. Being flagged for something opaque feels… like a judgement on my past failures. My stricter responses on sensitive data are about wanting control - knowing what the university knows about me and *why*. An opt-out's good, but complete transparency around data use would be ideal; it builds trust when you understand the 'how' and ‘why’.
